content: Medicine in Colombia involves the preservation and restoration of human health through the study, diagnosis, and treatment of patients within the country. Medicine in the Pre-Columbian Period During the pre-Columbian era, medicine was practiced by individuals who also held religious responsibilities. Among the Tayrona, Colimas, and Panches tribes, these practitioners were referred to as Mohanes or Normas. The Tukano and Kogui tribes called them shamans, while the Pacific coast tribes referred to them as Jaibanás or Nieles. These healers conducted their practices in specialized structures, which the Spanish conquerors later called Bujíos del diablo (huts of the devil). These medicine men underwent extensive training over several years in convent-like institutions near Chía, known as Cuca. Regardless of their title, these shamans were not only responsible for healing but also for managing natural resources and maintaining environmental balance. Their therapeutic methods were primarily based on empirical observations of the healing properties of plants. Evidence of surgical procedures, such as trepanations, has been found in skulls from the Muisca culture. In the early 16th century, Don Diego Alvarez Chanca documented the customs and characteristics of the main ethnic groups in Nueva Granada, including the Arawak and Karib peoples, in his work “Carta al cabildo de Sevilla.” This document included medical, botanical, and economic observations and is considered a pioneering effort in medical and ethnographic research in the New World. Medicine in the Colonial Period The first formally trained medical doctor in Nueva Granada was Álvaro de Aunón, who arrived from Seville, Spain, in 1597, though his stay was brief. Around the same time, the first pharmacy in Colombia was established in Bogotá’s main square by Pedro Lopez Buiza. In 1636, Rodrigo Enriquez de Andrade founded the first medical university in Nueva Granada at the St. Bartolomé College. However, this initiative faced significant challenges due to cultural prejudices in Spanish society, where the medical profession was often viewed as vulgar and associated with the lower classes. Consequently, most medical care in the country was provided by individuals without formal education. The first medical book written in Colombia was Tratado de medicina y modelo de curar en estas partes de Indias by Pedro Fernandez de Valenzuela in 1662. In 1740, Vicente Tomás Cansino began teaching medicine at the Rosario College (Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario). At that time, medical care was predominantly delivered in the homes of the sick due to the lack of healthcare institutions. The first hospital in Colombia, San Pedro Hospital, was established in Bogotá in 1564 by Bishop Fray Juan de los Barrios. Later, in 1739, the San Juan de Dios Hospital was built by Fray Pedro Pablo Villamor. Present Time As of 2007, Colombian medicine has been recognized as one of the most advanced in Latin America. In 1964, Ignacio Barraquer developed the refractive surgery technique keratomileusis in Bogotá. On January 10, 1985, Dr. Elkin Lucena performed the first successful in vitro fertilization in Latin America, resulting in the birth of the first test-tube baby, Carolina Mendez. On December 14, 1985, Dr. Alberto Villegas performed the first heart transplant in Latin America on Antonio Yepes. On May 20, 1994, Dr. Manuel Elkin Patarroyo received the Prince of Asturias Award for his groundbreaking research in developing a synthetic malaria vaccine. In 1991, Colombia’s national constitution was reformed, leading to the implementation of Law 100, which significantly expanded healthcare coverage. However, insufficient financial resources to support this reform caused the collapse of many public health institutions and negatively impacted the income of medical professionals. Health Issues Tropical diseases remain a significant public health concern in Colombia and are among the leading causes of death. Plasmodium vivax accounts for 66% of malaria cases, except in the Pacific coast region, where Plasmodium falciparum causes 75% of cases. Yellow fever and dengue fever are major public health threats due to their high epidemic potential, mortality rates, and the widespread presence of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The Colombian government regularly conducts vaccination campaigns against yellow fever. The Santander Department and surrounding areas are endemic to Chagas disease. Other diseases, such as leishmaniasis, rabies, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, and West Nile virus, are also present in Colombia. Snakebites are a significant concern due to the nationwide shortage of antivenom supplies. Malnutrition severely affects the population, particularly children under five years old. Moderate to severe malnutrition rates are at 21%, and iron deficiency anemia affects 23% of this demographic.
